summary: The note describes the Strike of the 100,000, an eight-day strike in German-occupied Belgium from 10 to 18 May 1941. It was led by Julien Lahaut, head of the Belgian Communist Party, even though the Nazi-Soviet Pact was still in force. The strike aimed to win a wage increase and also served as passive resistance to the German occupation.
one_line: An eight-day 1941 strike in German-occupied Belgium, led by Communist Party head Julien Lahaut, demanding higher wages and resisting the occupation.
key_facts: The Strike of the 100,000 was an 8-day strike in German-occupied Belgium.
The Strike of the 100,000 took place from 10–18 May 1941.
The strike was led by Julien Lahaut, head of the Belgian Communist Party.
The Belgian Communist Party is also known by its French name, Parti Communiste de Belgique (PCB).
The strike took place even though the Nazi—Soviet Pact was still in force.
The object of the strike was to demand a wage increase.
The strike was also an act of passive resistance to the German occupation.
